name: Burnt matchstick lashes

lead: Burnt matchstick lashes is a folk beauty trick in which the charred tip of a burnt match or other burnt wood is used to darken pale lashes and brows. The black residue stands in for mascara, giving the eyes a more defined look.

Darkening the lash line with soot or charcoal has deep roots: kohl and similar eye paints made partly from charcoal or soot go back thousands of years, and Victorian women mixed ash or lampblack at home for lashes.

paras: Practitioners describe letting the burnt tip cool, then lightly touching or brushing the black residue along the lashes. It is typically used as a stopgap when mascara is unavailable.

Match heads and soot are not cosmetic ingredients and are unsterile. Regulators and ophthalmology sources caution against non-cosmetic substances near the eye because of irritation and infection risk.

angle.text: The carbon deposit visibly darkens light lashes and brows, which is why it has been used as improvised mascara.

lead: Burnt matchstick lashes refers to using the charred end of a burnt match, or similar burnt wood, to darken the eyelashes and eyebrows as a stand-in for mascara. The black carbon residue deposits on the hair, making lashes look darker and fuller.

The idea sits in a long history of soot-based eye cosmetics. Kohl, used in ancient Egypt and elsewhere, was made from stibnite, galena or charcoal and soot, and in India kajal is traditionally made from soot of burned oil.[1][2] Wikipedia notes Victorian women made their own mascara by heating ash or lampblack with elderberry juice.[2]
No studies of match-based lash darkening exist; related health literature concerns kohl and other soot or metal-based eye products, some of which contained lead.[1]
infobox: Charred wood or match tip, soot

paras: The trick uses the carbon from burnt wood as a pigment. It is related to historical eye makeup made from soot and charcoal, such as kohl and kajal.[1][2]

Kohl has been used since about 3100 BCE in Egypt and spread across Africa, the Middle East and South Asia.[1] Victorian women mixed ash or lampblack at home for lashes; commercial products followed with Eugène Rimmel and, in 1915, Maybelline's early mascara.[2]

Lead-contaminated kohl has been linked to raised blood lead levels, and the US FDA does not approve kohl as a color additive.[1] Mascara safety discussions also cover allergies and microbial contamination.[2]

timeline.event: Thomas Lyle Williams makes mascara for his sister Mabel, leading to Maybelline.[2]
